questions.q: What is the main advantage of csv.DictReader over plain line.split(",")?
options: It deletes rows with missing values automatically
It correctly handles quoted fields with embedded commas, and lets you access values by column name instead of position
It automatically converts every value to the correct numeric type
It is the only way to open a file in Python
questions.explain: The csv module respects quoting rules a plain split ignores, and DictReader adds readable column-name access on top.

questions.q: In orders.csv, what did csv.DictReader reveal about order 1014?
options: Its quantity is -1, a data-entry error
Its customer_name is blank
Its unit_price is missing
It has a duplicate order_id
questions.explain: Order 1014 (Marcus Ibeh, Insulated Bottle 1L) has quantity -1 — you can't order negative one of something.

questions.q: Why does csv.DictWriter require an explicit fieldnames argument?
options: Unlike DictReader, it has no existing CSV to read column names and order from, so you must supply them
fieldnames controls which rows get written, not which columns
fieldnames is optional and rarely used in practice
It only accepts a single column name, never a list
questions.explain: DictReader infers fieldnames from the header row it reads; DictWriter is writing a new file, so there's no header to infer from.

questions.q: Why should open() be called with newline="" when reading or writing CSV files with the csv module?
options: It converts all fields to strings automatically
It's the documented, correct way to avoid extra blank rows appearing on some platforms
It is required only when the file has no header row
It makes the csv module run faster
questions.explain: Leaving newline="" off can produce incorrect row handling, particularly on Windows.

questions.q: When csv.DictReader reads the quantity column from orders.csv, what type is row["quantity"] before you convert it?
options: A Python list
An integer automatically
A float automatically
A string, like every other value DictReader returns
questions.explain: The csv module doesn't guess types — every field comes back as a string until you explicitly convert it, e.g. with int().
